messages.subject: help assessing dimensional invariance
parts:
Hello All,

I am stalled on this analysis and could use some insight!

I intend invariance testing of models between two groups, but am having trouble interpreting whether dimensional invariance is supported before I can proceed to any further testing.

The data are tricky ordinal data, some items with 3 response options and some with 4. I'm using estimator = "WLSM" and interpreting the robust (scaled) fit statistics.

There is both a 5 and 6 factor version of this model with fit statistics as shown below. The 6 factor model is the same as the 5 factor model for the first 5 factors, and adds an additional LV with 2 indicators.

 I am inclined to conclude that the models as specified (both the 5F and 6F versions) do not fit well in either sample. Mod indices are not helpful, suggest different things for the samples separately.

Also - I just read the Xia & Yang (2019) article and am now skeptical of RMSEA (too small) and TLI/CFI (too big).

I can't continue on the configural invariance testing, right? Because I can't support dimensional invariance?

For next steps does it make sense to fit a smaller/simpler model (e.g. 3 or 4 factors) and do the same thing?

Thanks for any advice!

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: help assessing dimensional invariance
parts: I can't continue on the configural invariance testing, right? Because I can't support dimensional invariance?

It sounds to me like these are already questions of configural invariance.  You can use a permutation test of configural invariance to test the H0 that (regardless of whether the hypothesized model fits well or poorly) the fit is equivalent across groups.

https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01455

As I recommend in the paper linked above, if there is no evidence against configural invariance, yet the model needs modification, then it should be modified simultaneously/identically in both groups.  From this perspective, you can fit your 3-, 4-, 5-, and 6-factor MG-CFAs to both samples, and for each one use semTools::permuteMeasEq() to verify the model is equally (in)valid across groups.  

Note that your larger sample is very large (N > 3000), so you have a lot of power to detect even trivial misfit.  If you are using WLSM (not -MV), then you should have access to the "Robust CFI" and "Robust RMSEA" rather than the "Scaled" versions (which merely use the standard formulas but replace chi-squared with the scaled test statistic).  I would trust those, and also refer to the whole 90% CI for RMSEA to see which null hypotheses (close, approximate, poor) cannot be rejected by the data.  Also, if models with more (hopefully, theoretically supported) dimensions do not lead to a good fit, then consider looking at lavResiduals() to see which specific relationships (in each group) the model fails to reproduce closely.  That may give you other ideas about how your model could be improved besides adding dimensions.
